# Presenting data effectively

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Learning objectives
By the end of this chapter you will be able to:

- choose between text, table, and figure for a given result
- design a baseline and a results table to journal standard
- report numbers with appropriate precision and confidence intervals
:::

Readers look at tables and figures before they read the text. Each one must stand alone, legible without flipping back to the methods. Together, they should carry the paper's main message for someone who reads only the abstract, skims the headings, and studies the figures.

## Choosing the right format

- **Text** when a result is one or two numbers and no comparison is needed ("Participants were mostly male, 2,829 (54%)").
- **Table** when exact values matter, or when readers may want to compare more than two or three numbers.
- **Figure** when the pattern, distribution, or trend matters more than individual values.

Never repeat the same result across text, table, and figure; most journals will flag duplicate reporting in review.

A worked example of why the format choice matters. @fig-overkill plots the same finding (*"participants were mostly male, 2,829 (54%)"*) as a pie chart and as a bar chart.

::: {#fig-overkill layout-ncol=2}

![A pie chart of a single proportion: two slices, one short sentence of information, several seconds of reader effort to estimate the angle.](../figures/sw/05-pie-overkill.png){#fig-pie-overkill fig-alt="A two-slice pie chart of a single proportion; the slices are close in size and hard to compare by angle."}

![A bar chart of the same proportion: two bars, the y-axis carries no extra meaning, and the reader still has to read the number off the label.](../figures/sw/06-bar-overkill.png){#fig-bar-overkill fig-alt="A two-bar chart of the same single proportion; the value is still read from the number label rather than the bar height."}

Both charts occupy valuable space to communicate a single number. The sentence *"Participants were mostly male, 2,829 (54%)"* conveys the same information in less space, with no risk of misreading.
:::

Rule of thumb: if a sentence will do the job, let it.

## Tables

Effective tables follow a few consistent rules. Avoid vertical lines. Use horizontal lines sparingly: top, bottom, and under the header is usually enough. Make the legend self-explanatory. Put units in the row or column labels, not in the cells. Keep decimal places consistent and proportionate to how precisely the variable was measured. Report group sizes in the header (`n = 242`) so every percentage is interpretable without arithmetic. Define any abbreviation in a footnote, even if it is already spelled out in the text.

A full worked example. The two tables below carry the same baseline characteristics of a (fictional) acute heart failure cohort, stratified by 30-day readmission. The first would not pass review; the second is close to what most journals expect.

**Avoid:**

| Variable    | Group 1               | Group 2                | p         |
|-------------|-----------------------|------------------------|-----------|
| Age (years) | 71.083 ± 11.61        | 69.734 ± 11.702        | 0.0043    |
| Gender      | 364 males, 302 females| 2,465 males, 2,073 females | 0.874 |
| Bmi         | 28.1 (24--31)         | 27.6                   | 0.45      |
| Smoking     | Yes 22% No 78%        | Yes 19% No 81%         | NS        |
| LVEF        | 40.41234              | 42.3                   | p = 0.000 |
| Prior HF    | 267/666 (40.090%)     | 1219/4538 (26.862%)    | p<.001    |

Problems: spurious precision (`71.083`, `40.090%`); inconsistent labels (`Gender`, `Bmi`); missing units on BMI and LVEF; mixed formats inside a single column; `NS` with no number; `p = 0.000` (no p-value is literally zero); `p<.001` missing both the leading zero and the space around the operator; missing thousands separator in `4538`; group sizes not in the header, forcing the reader to recompute percentages; the category label `Gender` describes a variable that is actually sex at birth, which many journals now distinguish.

**Prefer:**

| Characteristic                           | Readmitted (n = 666) | Not readmitted (n = 4,538) | p        |
|------------------------------------------|----------------------|----------------------------|----------|
| Age (years), mean ± SD                   | 71.1 ± 11.6          | 69.7 ± 11.7                | 0.004    |
| Male sex, n (%)                          | 364 (54.7)           | 2,465 (54.3)               | 0.87     |
| BMI (kg/m²), median (IQR)                | 28.1 (24.6--31.4)    | 27.6 (24.1--31.0)          | 0.45     |
| Current smoker, n (%)                    | 147 (22.1)           | 862 (19.0)                 | 0.06     |
| NYHA class III--IV, n (%)                | 409 (61.4)           | 2,261 (49.8)               | <0.001   |
| LVEF (%), mean ± SD                      | 40.4 ± 13.5          | 42.3 ± 13.2                | <0.001   |
| NT-proBNP at discharge (pg/mL), median (IQR) | 1,194 (671--2,186) | 945 (513--1,710)         | <0.001   |
| eGFR (mL/min/1.73 m²), median (IQR)      | 56 (42--72)          | 58 (43--73)                | 0.11     |
| Prior HF admission, n (%)                | 267 (40.1)           | 1,219 (26.9)               | <0.001   |
| Atrial fibrillation, n (%)               | 221 (33.2)           | 1,539 (33.9)               | 0.71     |

: Baseline characteristics by 30-day readmission, simulated acute heart failure cohort (n = 5,204). NT-proBNP available for 5,065 patients (646 readmitted, 4,419 not). {tbl-colwidths="[38,20,26,16]"}

Improvements: decimals consistent and proportionate to measurement precision; units in the variable labels; `n (%)` for every categorical variable; medians with IQR for skewed variables (BMI, eGFR, NT-proBNP, the latter always reported on a skewed scale); group sizes in the header; p-values reported to two or three decimals, or `<0.001` when smaller; precise category labels (`Male sex`); rows ordered by a clinically intuitive logic (demographics, anthropometry, behaviour, severity, biomarkers, comorbidity); and the non-significant rows (male sex, eGFR, atrial fibrillation) reported with their actual p-values rather than dropped, so the reader sees what did not differ as well as what did.

## Results tables

A baseline table describes the sample; a results table carries the analysis, and it follows different rules. A multivariable model gets one row per predictor, and each row needs the effect estimate, its 95% confidence interval, and the p-value. Report the estimate on its natural scale (odds ratio, hazard ratio, mean difference), state the per-unit contrast for continuous predictors, and name the reference category for every categorical one. Put the outcome, the model, and the denominator in the title, once, rather than repeating them down the rows.

| Predictor                    | Adjusted OR (95% CI) | p       |
|------------------------------|----------------------|---------|
| NT-proBNP (per log-unit)     | 1.25 (1.14--1.38)    | <0.001  |
| Age (per 10 years)           | 1.06 (0.98--1.14)    | 0.14    |
| Male sex (vs female)         | 0.98 (0.83--1.16)    | 0.83    |
| LVEF (per 5%)                | 0.95 (0.92--0.98)    | 0.002   |
| NYHA III--IV (vs I--II)      | 1.67 (1.41--1.99)    | <0.001  |

: Multivariable logistic regression for 30-day readmission (complete-case, n = 5,065). Reference categories: female sex, NYHA I--II. {tbl-colwidths="[46,30,24]"}

The intercept is not a finding; omit it. Do not report a predictor as significant in the table and then discuss a different unadjusted number in the text — the table and the prose must name the same estimate. And do not print the same estimates in a table, a figure, and the running text: choose the one that does the work and cross-reference it from the others. A table earns its place when the reader needs exact values — a confidence interval a regulator will check, a number a later meta-analysis will extract. A figure earns its place when the reader needs a pattern, such as a monotonic gradient across quartiles. When both are true, the figure carries the message and the table goes to the supplement.

## Reporting numbers

Precision matters more than volume. A few rules avoid most problems in peer review.

- **Decimals.** Match the measurement precision. Age to one decimal; p-values to two or three; percentages to one decimal when n is small. More digits than the data supports looks unserious (`67.423 years` implies you know age in seconds).
- **p-values.** Two decimals when p ≥ 0.01. Three decimals when 0.001 ≤ p < 0.01. Below that, report `<0.001`. Never `p = 0.000`. Never `NS`; give the actual number so the reader can judge.
- **Estimate + 95% CI with every p-value.** A p-value says whether a difference is unlikely by chance; it does not say whether it is clinically meaningful. Report the estimate (mean difference, OR, HR, RR) with its confidence interval.
- **Statistical significance is not clinical importance.** A finding can be statistically significant and clinically trivial (e.g. *"mean LDL fell by 0.03 mmol/L (95% CI 0.01--0.05, p = 0.002)"* is significant and clinically negligible), or clinically meaningful but not statistically significant in an underpowered study. Use "significant" only when you mean statistical significance, and always pair it with the effect size so the reader can judge [@motulsky2014misconceptions].
- **Missing data.** State the denominator for every analysis. If 139 of 5,204 participants have a missing NT-proBNP value, say so (`NT-proBNP available for 5,065 of 5,204 patients, 97.3%`) and describe how you handled the missingness (complete-case, multiple imputation). STROBE item 12 covers this.
- **Units.** SI units for laboratory values (μmol/L, mmol/L) unless the target journal specifies otherwise, and consistent throughout the paper.

## Graphs

The principles of good data visualisation are rooted in Edward Tufte's core insight: maximise the ratio of data to ink, and eliminate everything that does not help the reader understand the data [@tufte2001visual]. Common errors include truncated axes that exaggerate small differences, dual y-axes that create misleading visual correlations, unnecessary 3D effects, and pie charts with too many categories. Avoid bar charts for continuous outcomes; a boxplot, violin plot, or strip plot shows the distribution, not just the mean with an error bar.

Claus Wilke's taxonomy of bad figures is useful here [@wilke2019fundamentals]. An *ugly* figure has aesthetic problems but is otherwise clear. A *bad* figure has problems related to perception: it is confusing, misleading, or overcomplicated. A *wrong* figure is mathematically incorrect. All three deserve attention during revision.

Accessibility matters. Roughly 8% of men have some form of colour vision deficiency [@birch2012diagnosis]. Use colour palettes designed for universal readability ([viridis](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/viridis/vignettes/intro-to-viridis.html) and [ColorBrewer](https://colorbrewer2.org/) are reliable choices), and do not rely on colour alone to distinguish categories. Duplicate colour distinctions with shape, line style, or pattern.

::: {.column-margin}
Part II goes deeper. [Principles of data visualisation](10-principles.qmd) develops the principles here into a full taxonomy. [Chart types](11-chart-types.qmd) surveys chart types by data structure. [Pitfalls](12-pitfalls.qmd) works through seven paired failure modes with corrected examples.
:::

::: {#fig-wilke layout-ncol=2}

![**Ugly.** Harsh red/green defaults, lowercase axis labels, no units. Accurate, but unpublishable.](../figures/sw/01-ugly.png){#fig-ugly fig-alt="A bar chart with harsh red and green bars, lowercase axis labels, and no units."}

![**Bad.** Bar chart with SD error bars on a right-skewed biomarker. The distribution is log-normal; the bars imply a symmetric sampling distribution that does not exist here.](../figures/sw/02-bad-bar.png){#fig-bad-bar fig-alt="A bar chart with symmetric standard-deviation error bars on a right-skewed biomarker, implying a symmetry the data lack."}

![**Bad.** The y-axis starts at 500, not at zero. The medians differ 2.5-fold (1,873 vs 764 pg/mL); the bars drawn above them differ five-fold. Truncation has doubled the apparent effect.](../figures/sw/03-bad-truncated.png){#fig-bad-trunc fig-alt="A bar chart whose y-axis starts at 500 rather than zero, so two medians that differ two-and-a-half-fold are drawn as bars differing five-fold."}

![**Good.** Boxplot with jittered raw data, log-scaled y-axis (appropriate for a right-skewed biomarker), accessible two-colour palette, and a caption that makes the figure self-contained.](../figures/sw/04-good.png){#fig-good fig-alt="A boxplot with jittered raw data points on a log-scaled y-axis in a two-colour accessible palette, showing the biomarker distribution by group."}

NT-proBNP at discharge by 30-day readmission status (simulated). All four panels are drawn from one illustrative sample of 200 per group, so the failure modes can be compared on identical data; the numbers differ from the full-cohort descriptives tabulated above.
:::

## Figure legends

Figure legends are part of the figure, not the text. A reader who sees only the figure must understand what it shows, on whom, and how it was analysed. A complete legend includes:

- a short title (what is being shown);
- a description of groups or conditions (what each colour, line, or symbol means);
- the statistical test, and which groups are being compared;
- the sample size for each group;
- definitions of any abbreviations or symbols.

Keep interpretation out of the legend. *"Kaplan–Meier curves for 30-day readmission after acute heart failure, stratified by NT-proBNP at discharge (above vs below the cohort median). Log-rank test. n = 2,533 and 2,532; 139 patients with no NT-proBNP value are excluded."* belongs in the legend. *"Showing that NT-proBNP identifies high-risk patients at discharge..."* belongs in the results and discussion.

::: {.column-margin}
Figures for **posters** and **oral presentations** follow different conventions: larger type, fewer panels, one take-home per slide or panel. I have written short guides on both in the *Breathe* journal's *Doing Science* series: posters [@jacinto2013poster] and oral presentations [@jacinto2014oral].
:::

## Practice: fix the reporting

The results sentence below has four reporting problems. Find them before revealing the answer.

> *"Mortality was 12.812% in the treated group versus 8.1% in controls (p = 0.000), a significant reduction. LVEF was 34.56789 ± 11."*

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answer

1. **Spurious precision.** 12.812% and 34.56789 imply an accuracy the data cannot support; one decimal is enough.
2. **`p = 0.000`.** No p-value is literally zero; report `< 0.001`.
3. **No effect estimate with a confidence interval.** The mortality difference needs an absolute or relative measure with a 95% CI, not two percentages and a p-value.
4. **"Significant" as if it meant important, plus a units/precision mismatch.** "Significant reduction" states statistical significance where the reader needs the effect size; and LVEF is given without units (%) and with inconsistent precision (34.6 ± 11).
:::
